'''''Aquilegia chrysantha''''', the '''golden columbine''', is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[flowering plant]] native to the southwestern [[United States]] and northwestern [[Mexico]].<ref name="POWO"/> The plant, with a height of between {{convert|40|cm|in}} and {{convert|120|cm|in}}, has yellow flowers. ''A. chrysantha''. as with other members of the ''[[Aquilegia coerulea]]'' [[species complex]], is evolved for pollination by [[Sphingidae|hawkmoth]]. It favors moist environments in its mountainous range.

In gardens, a [[cultivar]] of the species known as 'Yellow Queen' is known for its appearance and won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]. Hybrids utilizing ''A. chrysantha'', particularly those with ''[[Aquilegia coerulea]]'', are especially popular. Both wild and cultivated ''A. chrysantha'', known for their large flowers, require moist and well-drained soil.

== Description ==
[[File:Aquilegia chrysantha 2018-06-07 3298.jpg|thumb|right|alt=Aquilegia chrysantha leaves|Leaves of ''A. chrysantha'']]
The ferny leaves have three leaflets with three lobes and grow from the base and off the flowering stems. The flowers grow on a long stem above the leaves and have five pointed yellow [[sepal]]s and five yellow [[petal]]s with long spurs of around {{cvt|6.7|cm}}<ref name="Miller"/> projecting backwards between the sepals.<ref name="RHSPF"/> Its sepals of {{convert|20|mm|in}} to {{convert|35|mm|in}} can be spreading, [[lanceolate]], or somewhat oval.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|75}} At the center of the flower are many yellow [[stamen]]s.<ref name="RHSPF"/> The height of the plant's flowering stems range from {{convert|40|cm|in}} to {{convert|120|cm|in}} tall. Flowers are golden yellow.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|75}}

At the earliest, the plant achieves maturity in two years under cultivation. It is [[polycarpic]], dropping seeds several times during its lifespan,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Age of Maturity and Life Span in Herbaceous, Polycarpic Perennials|jstor=4354373|journal=Botanical Review|first1=Martin H.|last1=Bender|first2=Jerry M.|last2=Baskin|first3=Carol C.|last3=Baskin|date=2000|page=339|volume=66|number=3|doi=10.1007/BF02868921 |bibcode=2000BotRv..66..311B }}</ref> which is longer than other ''Aquilegia'' species.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|18}} Breeding is performed through its [[unisexual flowers]], meaning that individual flowers exclusively possess either [[stamen]] or [[carpel]]s, making it [[monoecious]].<ref name=Johnson2/> ''A. chrysantha'' is similar to the also yellow ''[[Aquilegia flavescens]]'' but the former is more resistant to droughts and blooms longer.<ref>{{cite book|title=Water Wise: Native Plants for Intermountain Landscapes|first1=Wendy|last1=Mee|first2=Jared|last2=Barnes|first3=Roger|last3=Kjelgren|first4=Teresa|last4=Cerny|first5=Craig|last5=Johnson|chapter=Forbs|page=79|doi=10.2307/j.ctt5vkjtx.7|jstor=j.ctt5vkjtx.7|date=2003|publisher=[[University Press of Colorado]]|isbn=978-0-87421-561-8 }}</ref> Pollination is primarily performed by moths, butterflies, and bees. Blooming occurs April and September, with a peak varying between late spring and late summer.<ref name=Johnson2/>

The plant needs moist, well-drained areas to succeed. Poor drainage can cause the [[root crown]] to rot. Excessive heat increases the plant's risk to [[aphid]]s and [[spider mite]]s. Overly warm periods can result in the plant going dormant.<ref name=Johnson2/>

In the variety ''hinckleyana'', leaves grow into two parts and pedal blades range between only {{convert|2|cm|in}} long and {{convert|16|mm|in}} wide.<ref name=Johnson2>{{cite web|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=AQCH|title=''Aquilegia chrysantha''|website=wildflower.org|publisher=[[Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center]]|access-date=December 2, 2024}}</ref> In wild specimens observed in southern Arizona during May and June 1980, plants generally exhibited a faint scent. One plant observed during that period was found with the same pattern of pink sepals and spurs with yellow pedals as found in certain ''[[Aquilegia micrantha]]'' populations of [[Colorado]] and [[Utah]].<ref name="Miller"/>

== Taxonomy ==
''Aquilegia chrysantha'' is part of the ''[[Aquilegia coerulea]]'' [[species complex]] adapted for [[Sphingidae|hawkmoth]] pollination.<ref name="Fior"/> Both species are native to the western United States and evolved to have longer nectar spurs than those on eastern U.S. hummingbird-pollinated species as hawkmoths have longer tongues than hummingbirds.<ref>{{cite book|title=Spring Wildflowers of the Northeast: A Natural History|first=Carol|last=Gracie|publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]|location=[[Princeton, New Jersey|Princeton, NJ]]|date=2012|isbn=978-0-691-19953-5|page=40}}</ref> ''A. chrysantha'' belongs to a likely [[Monophyly|monophyletic]] group with the other [[North America]]n columbine species, which diverged from their closest relatives in [[East Asia]] in the mid-[[Pliocene]] around 3.8 million years ago.<ref name="Fior"/> North of the [[Grand Canyon]], ''A. chrysantha'' [[Intergradation|intergrades]] with ''A. coerulea'' var. ''pinetorum''.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|75}} In Texas, ''A. chrysantha'' intergrades with ''[[Aquilegia longissima]]''.<ref name="Miller"/>

The species was first assigned the [[binomial nomenclature]] ''Aquilegia chrysantha'' in 1873. Its [[type locality (biology)|type locality]] is in the [[Organ Mountains]] of [[New Mexico]].<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|75}} 

The closely related ''[[Aquilegia chaplinei]]'' is considered a dwarf version of ''A. chrysantha'' that is better suited to arid environments.<ref name=Nold>{{cite book|title=Columbines: ''Aquilegia'', ''Paraquilegia'', and ''Semiaquilegia''|first=Robert|last=Nold|publisher=Timber Press|date=2003|location=[[Portland, Oregon|Portland]], [[Oregon|OR]]|isbn=0881925888|url=https://archive.org/details/columbines00robe|url-access=registration|via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref>{{rp|74}}<ref name=Payson>{{cite journal|title=The North American Species of Aquilegia|journal=[[Contributions from the United States National Herbarium]]|volume=20|number=4|date=1918|jstor=23492230 |last=Payson |first=Edwin Blake |author-link=Edwin Blake Payson |pages=I–IX |jstor-access=free}}</ref>{{rp|157}} In 1985, Emily J. Lott proposed reclassifying ''A. chaplinei'' as ''Aquilegia chrysantha'' var. ''chaplinei'' in the journal ''[[Phytologia]]''. Lott's proposal came out of her study of plants in the [[Chihuahuan Desert]], stemming from her 1979 unpublished master's thesis on ''Aquilegia'' in the [[Trans-Pecos]] region of Texas.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://archive.org/details/biostor-208336|title=New combinations in Chihuahuan Desert ''Aquilegia'' (Ranunculaceae)|first=Emily J.|last=Lott|journal=[[Phytologia]]|date=1985 |page=488|volume=58}}</ref> The name proposed by Lott was not broadly accepted outside of Texas,<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|74}} where it is used by the [[Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center]] of the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref name=Johnson>{{cite web|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=AQCHC|title=''Aquilegia chrysantha'' var. ''chaplinei''|website=wildflower.org|publisher=[[Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center]]|access-date=December 2, 2024}}</ref>

The nectar spurs present ''Aquilegia'' species are an unusual evolutionary trait. The genus has radiated widely since its relatively recent origin. In order to determine the gene responsible for the trait, a 2020 paper by researchers from the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]], [[Harvard University]], and [[Stanford University]] utilized ''A. chrysantha'' (alongside ''A. coerulea'', ''[[Aquilegia formosa]]'', and ''[[Aquilegia sibirica]]'') as a spurred ''Aquilegia'' taxa to compare against the sole spurless ''Aquilegia'' species, ''[[Aquilegia ecalcarata]]''. This research identified a gene named ''POPVICH'' (''POP'') as responsible for cell proliferation during the early stage of spur development. ''POP'' appeared at higher levels in the pedals of the spurred ''Aquilegia'' studied than those of the spurless ''A. ecalcarata''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=''POPOVICH'', encoding a C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor, plays a central role in the development of a key innovation, floral nectar spurs, in ''Aquilegia''|first1=Evangeline S.|last1=Ballerini|first2=Ya|last2=Min|first3=Molly B.|last3=Edwards|first4=Elena M.|last4=Kramer|first5=Scott A.|last5=Hodges|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]|volume=117|number=36|date=September 8, 2020|pages=22552–22553|doi=10.1073/pnas.2006912117 |doi-access=free |jstor=26969162|pmid=32848061 |pmc=7486772 |bibcode=2020PNAS..11722552B }}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
The word ''[[wikt:columbine|columbine]]'' derives from the Latin word {{lang|la|[[wikt:columbinus|columbinus]]}}, meaning "dove", a reference to the flowers' appearance of a group of doves. The genus name ''[[wikt:Aquilegia|Aquilegia]]'' comes from the Latin word for "eagle", {{lang|la|[[wikt:aquila|aquila]]}}, in reference to the pedals' resemblance to eagle talons.<ref name=Johnson2/> The specific epithet ''[[wikt:chrysantha|chrysantha]]'' is [[Latin]] for "golden-flowered".<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|75}}

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Sugarloaf Peak, Organ Mountains, New Mexico (2007).jpg|thumb|The Organ Mountains in New Mexico, where ''A. chrysantha''{{apostrophe}}s type locality is]]
The species is native to the southwestern United States from extreme southern Utah to [[Texas]], including [[Arizona]], Colorado, and New Mexico, and to [[Sonora]], [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], [[Coahuila]], and [[Nuevo Leon]] in northwestern Mexico.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=Johnson2/> It grows in moist habitats in mountainous regions. The plant's native elevation range is between {{convert|910|m|ft}} and {{convert|3350|m|ft}} above sea level.<ref name="Miller"/>

The population of ''A. chrysantha'' in south-central Colorado is unusually disjunct from the rest of the species's range. This population usually possess smaller flowers. They have sepals extending only {{convert|10|mm|in}} to {{convert|18|mm|in}} long and spurs only {{convert|35|mm|in}} to {{convert|40|mm|in}} long. This population is sometimes recognized as a separate variety, ''A. chrysantha'' var. ''rydbergii'', but this distinction is not recognized in the ''[[Flora of North America]]''.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|75}}

In 1881, botanist [[Thomas Meehan (botanist)|Thomas Meehan]] noted the apparent proliferation of ''A. chysantha'' in the [[Colorado Springs]] area, particularly around [[Cheyenne Cañon]] and [[Glen Eyrie]], since botanists had examined the area in 1871 and 1873. Meehan theorized that their rapid spread was partially due to the increased human habitation of the area altering environmental circumstance.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Aquilegia chrysantha|journal=[[International Journal of Plant Sciences|Botanical Gazette]]|first=Thomas|last=Meehan|author-link=Thomas Meehan (botanist)|volume=6|number=8|date=August 1881|pages=247–248|doi=10.1086/325502 |jstor=2994269}}</ref>

A population of columbines from the [[Baboquivari Mountains]] of southern Arizona has been the subject of debate regarding its speciation. While occasionally described as a variety of ''A. chrysantha'', it has also been classified as part of the species ''A. longissima''.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|75}}

== Cultivation ==
''A. chrysantha'' succeeds well in a variety of soils when provided adequate moisture, drainage, and shade.<ref name=Johnson2/> It is recognized for its large flowers, is the parent to a number of garden hybrids. Some, such as the white 'Alba', were given pseudo-botanical names in the 19th century. Additionally, from the Baboquivari population have been collected and privately cultivated.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|75–76}}

The [[cultivar]] 'Yellow Queen' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHSPF"/> Often sold as ''A. chrysantha'', 'Yellow Queen' is recognized for its massive yellow flowers and long life.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|76}} 'Yellow Queen' has a tendency to produce more flowers than the standard ''A. chrysantha''.<ref>{{cite book|title=Encyclopedia of Perennials|editor-last1=Rice|editor-first1=Graham|editor-last2=Bluemel|editor-first2=Kurt|publisher=[[American Horticultural Society]], [[DK (publisher)|DK Publishing]]|location=New York|date=2006|isbn=9780756613433|page=65}}</ref> The cultivar prefers moist, well-drained soil of clay, sand, or loam. Flowers bloom May and June in the northern hemisphere, with darker yellow center pedals.<ref name="RHSPF"/>

Crosses between ''A. coerulea'' and ''A. chrysantha''{{snd}} and possibly ''A. formosa'' for the addition of red{{snd}} are considered the most valuable hybrids. Showing characteristics of both species, they possess relatively short lifespans. Seed availability of these plants is relatively high in North America.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|137}} ''Aquilegia'' x ''jaeschkanii'', thought to be a cross between ''A. chrysantha'' and ''[[Aquilegia skinneri]]'', is a less valued hybrid.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|136}}

In 1916, botanist [[Theodore D. A. Cockerell]] described an [[F1 hybrid]] that his wife, [[Wilmatte P. Cockerell]], had made between ''A. chrysantha'' and ''[[Aquilegia desertorum]]''. He observed that the coloration and time of flowering were both indeterminate. The flowers of F1 ''A. desertorum'' x ''chrysantha'', though less reminiscent of the parent species and more characteristic of species in the ''[[Aquilegia vulgaris]]'' group, had a width more typical of ''A. chrysantha''. He also noted the longstanding presence of ''A. chrysantha ''x ''A. coerulea'' hybrids in gardens; this hybrid's flowers are paler than ''A. coerulea'' with yellow coloring.<ref>{{cite journal|title=A New Hybrid Columbine|journal=[[International Journal of Plant Sciences|Botanical Gazette]]|volume=62|number=5|date=November 1916|pages=413–414|jstor=2468994|first=Theodore D. A.|last=Cockerell|doi=10.1086/331951 |author-link=Theodore D. A. Cockerell}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
''Aquilegia chrysantha'' flowers in May and early June. It is chiefly pollinated by the hawkmoth species ''[[Eumorpha achemon]]'', the Achemon sphinx moth, and also by moths of the ''[[Sphinx (genus)|Sphinx]]'' genus. It is occasionally visited by large [[bee]]s and [[hummingbird]]s.<ref name="Miller"/>

== Conservation ==
{{As of|2024|October}}, [[NatureServe]] did not give a worldwide or United States-wide [[NatureServe conservation status|conservation status]] for ''A. chrysantha''. In individual states, it is listed as Critically Imperiled (S1) in Utah, Imperiled (S2) in Colorado and Nevada, Vulnerable (S3) in Arizona and New Mexico, and is given no status rank (SNR) in Texas.<ref name="NatureServe"/>
